title: Forces come in pairs
scope: Choose the objectives in your school’s topic list. These are original practice questions with illustrative values, not a claim of an official school paper format.

objectives.label: Explain and use resultant force.
objectives.note: The vector sum of the forces acting on one chosen object.

objectives.label: Use moments and the principle of moments; explain stability.
objectives.note: The turning effect of a force about a pivot, equal to force times perpendicular distance.

objectives.label: Explain and use acceleration and resultant force.
objectives.note: For constant mass in this model, resultant force equals mass multiplied by acceleration.

objectives.label: Explain and use contact force.
objectives.note: A surface can exert a force on an object touching it.

objectives.label: Explain and use spring constant.
objectives.note: For a proportional spring, force divided by extension gives its spring constant.

objectives.label: Explain and use third-law pair.
objectives.note: Two interacting objects exert equal-magnitude opposite-direction forces on each other.

objectives.label: Explain and use momentum.
objectives.note: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity; a system’s total momentum is conserved when its external resultant impulse is zero.

objectives.label: Distinguish mass from weight and use W = mg.
objectives.note: Mass is measured in kg; weight is a gravitational force in N and depends on local g.

cards.definition: The vector sum of the forces acting on one chosen object.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A model cart has two horizontal forces: a motor pulls right and resistance is 19 N left. Its resultant is 28 N right. Calculate the motor force. Motor force − 19 N = 28 N. Motor force = 28 + 19 = 47 N.
cards.confusion: Forces on different objects do not cancel in a single-object force diagram.
cards.question: Explain resultant force from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: The vector sum of the forces acting on one chosen object. Forces on different objects do not cancel in a single-object force diagram.

cards.definition: The turning effect of a force about a pivot, equal to force times perpendicular distance.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A door needs a turning moment of 8.4 N m about its hinge. You push at right angles 0.70 m from the hinge. Calculate the required force. Force = moment ÷ perpendicular distance. 8.4 ÷ 0.70 = 12 N.
cards.confusion: Use perpendicular distance to the line of action, not an arbitrary length.
cards.question: Explain moment from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: The turning effect of a force about a pivot, equal to force times perpendicular distance. Use perpendicular distance to the line of action, not an arbitrary length.

cards.definition: For constant mass in this model, resultant force equals mass multiplied by acceleration.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A model lift has a constant mass. A resultant upward force of 18 N gives an upward acceleration of 1.5 m/s². Calculate the mass. Mass = resultant force ÷ acceleration. 18 ÷ 1.5 = 12 kg.
cards.confusion: Use the resultant force, not just one of several forces.
cards.question: Explain acceleration and resultant force from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: For constant mass in this model, resultant force equals mass multiplied by acceleration. Use the resultant force, not just one of several forces.

cards.definition: A surface can exert a force on an object touching it.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A rigid shelf supports a vase. Explain why “the shelf is not alive” does not prevent it exerting a force. Small deformations and interactions within the material produce contact forces. Being alive is not a condition for exerting a force.
cards.confusion: A table need not visibly move to exert an upward force.
cards.question: Explain contact force from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: A surface can exert a force on an object touching it. A table need not visibly move to exert an upward force.

cards.definition: For a proportional spring, force divided by extension gives its spring constant.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A proportional spring in a model force meter has spring constant 160 N/m. Calculate the extension produced by a 6.4 N force. Extension = force ÷ spring constant. 6.4 ÷ 160 = 0.040 m.
cards.confusion: Extension is the change in length, not the full stretched length.
cards.question: Explain spring constant from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: For a proportional spring, force divided by extension gives its spring constant. Extension is the change in length, not the full stretched length.

cards.definition: Two interacting objects exert equal-magnitude opposite-direction forces on each other.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A lorry and a small car interact during a collision. Compare their interaction force magnitudes. Explain why their accelerations or damage can nevertheless differ. The two interaction forces have equal magnitude. Their accelerations and damage can differ because mass and structure differ.
cards.confusion: The pair acts on different objects, so it does not balance the forces on either object by itself.
cards.question: Explain third-law pair from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: Two interacting objects exert equal-magnitude opposite-direction forces on each other. The pair acts on different objects, so it does not balance the forces on either object by itself.

cards.definition: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity; a system’s total momentum is conserved when its external resultant impulse is zero.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A model cart has momentum 10.8 kg m/s west and mass 3.6 kg. Calculate its speed and state its velocity direction. Speed = momentum magnitude ÷ mass. 10.8 ÷ 3.6 = 3.0 m/s. Its velocity is directed west.
cards.confusion: Choose the system and a direction before adding momenta.
cards.question: Explain momentum from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity; a system’s total momentum is conserved when its external resultant impulse is zero. Choose the system and a direction before adding momenta.

cards.definition: Mass measures inertia/amount of matter; weight is the gravitational force on a mass.
cards.explanation: Mass measures inertia/amount of matter; weight is the gravitational force on a mass.
cards.example: A 6 kg object weighs 60 N where g = 10 N/kg.
cards.confusion: Moving an object to weaker gravity changes its weight, not its mass.
cards.question: Explain mass and weight from memory and give its important distinction.
cards.answer: Mass measures inertia/amount of matter; weight is the gravitational force on a mass. Moving an object to weaker gravity changes its weight, not its mass.
cards.unit: kg for mass; N for weight

cards.definition: For rotational equilibrium, total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment about the chosen pivot.
cards.explanation: For rotational equilibrium, total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment about the chosen pivot.
cards.example: A smaller force can balance a larger force by acting farther from the pivot.
cards.confusion: Zero resultant force alone does not ensure rotational equilibrium.
cards.question: Explain principle of moments from memory and give its important distinction.
cards.answer: For rotational equilibrium, total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment about the chosen pivot. Zero resultant force alone does not ensure rotational equilibrium.
cards.formula: Σ clockwise moments = Σ anticlockwise moments

cards.definition: The centre of gravity is the point at which the whole weight may be treated as acting in a uniform gravitational field.
cards.explanation: The centre of gravity is the point at which the whole weight may be treated as acting in a uniform gravitational field.
cards.example: A wide-based, low object needs a larger tilt to bring its weight line beyond its base.
cards.confusion: Weight acts through the centre of gravity; a toppling threshold concerns that line’s position relative to the base.
cards.question: Explain centre of gravity and stability from memory and give its important distinction.
cards.answer: The centre of gravity is the point at which the whole weight may be treated as acting in a uniform gravitational field. Weight acts through the centre of gravity; a toppling threshold concerns that line’s position relative to the base.
